## Problem 1

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)

birthday_match = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

birthday_results =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    shared_birthday = map_lgl(group_size, birthday_match)
  ) |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(
    probability = mean(shared_birthday)
  )

birthday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  )
```

The probability of sharing a birthday increases as the group size increases. With around 23 people, the probability is about 50%. By 50 people, the probability is approximately 97%.

## Problem 2

```{r}
full_df =
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data/"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |>
mutate(data = map(path, \(x) read_csv(x, show_col_types = FALSE)))|>
  unnest(cols = data)
```


```{r}
tidy_df =
  full_df |>
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    arm = str_sub(files, 1, 3)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |>
  select(arm, subject_id = files, week, outcome)

tidy_df
```


```{r}
tidy_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subject_id, color = arm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~arm) +
  labs(
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome"
  )
```

The control group stays relatively stable over time, while the experimental group shows an increasing trend. There is some variation between subjects in both groups.


## Problem 3

```{r}
set.seed(1)

sim_ttest = function(mu) {
  sim_data =
    tibble(
      x = rnorm(30, mean = mu, sd = 5)
    )

  t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

sim_results =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    test_results = map(true_mu, sim_ttest)
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = test_results)
```

```{r}
power_df =
  sim_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(p.value < 0.05)
  )

power_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "True Mu",
    y = "Power"
  )
```

As the true mean increases, the power of the test also increases. When the true mean is 0, power is around 0.05. As the effect size gets larger, power approaches 1.


```{r}
mean_df =
  sim_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate)
  )

mean_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = mean_estimate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "True Mu",
    y = "Average Estimated Mu"
  )
```


```{r}
rejected_df =
  sim_results |>
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate)
  )

rejected_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = mean_estimate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "True Mu",
    y = "Average Estimated Mu (Rejected Only)"
  )
```

Not always. When the true mean is small and positive, the average estimate among rejected tests is higher than the true mean because larger estimates are more likely to reject the null. As the true mean increases the average estimate gets closer to the true value.
